questions.stem: Although Dutch speakers are a majority in Belgium as a whole, they are a minority in the capital city of Brussels. Work out, step by step in about 75 words, how the language pattern of the country differs from that of the capital, and what this means for the numeric strength of the Dutch speakers.

markingPoints.description: In the country as a whole 59 per cent of the population lives in the Flemish region and speaks Dutch, so the Dutch speakers are the majority
In Brussels 80 per cent of people speak French while 20 per cent are Dutch-speaking
So the Dutch speakers are a minority in the capital
The Dutch speakers' numeric majority does not hold in Brussels
Their numeric strength works for them at country level but not in the capital

answerScheme.modelAnswer: 1. In the country as a whole the Dutch speakers are the majority: 59 per cent of the population lives in the Flemish region and speaks Dutch. 2. In Brussels the position is reversed: 80 per cent of people speak French while 20 per cent are Dutch-speaking. 3. So the Dutch speakers form a minority in the capital. 4. Their numeric majority is therefore a strength at country level, not in Brussels itself.

questions.stem:
Belgium's population is not spread evenly across its language groups. Of the country's total population, 59 per cent lives in the Flemish region and speaks Dutch. Another 40 per cent people live in the Wallonia region and speak French, and the remaining one per cent of the Belgians speak German. The capital city Brussels breaks this pattern: 80 per cent of its people speak French while 20 per cent are Dutch-speaking. So the Dutch-speaking people are a majority in the country as a whole, but a minority in the capital.

(a) What share of Belgium's population lives in the Wallonia region, and which language do those people speak? (b) In the capital city Brussels, which language group is in the minority? (c) Explain why the Dutch community cannot simply take advantage of its numeric majority there and force its will on the French-speaking population.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: (a) 40 per cent live in the Wallonia region and speak French. (b) The Dutch speakers, at 20 per cent. (c) Brussels reverses the national pattern, so the Dutch speakers are only a minority there and cannot force their will on the French speakers.

questions.stem:
Sri Lanka is an island nation just a few kilometres off the southern coast of Tamil Nadu, with about two crore people, about the same as in Haryana. Like other nations in the South Asia region, it has a diverse population. The major social groups are the Sinhala-speakers, at 74 per cent, and the Tamil-speakers, at 18 per cent. Among the Tamils there are two sub-groups: Tamil natives of the country are called Sri Lankan Tamils (13 per cent), and the rest, whose forefathers came from India as plantation workers during the colonial period, are called Indian Tamils. Sri Lankan Tamils are concentrated in the north and east of the country.

(a) What share of Sri Lanka's population speaks Tamil, and into how many sub-groups are Tamil-speakers divided? (b) Name the sub-group whose forefathers came from India as plantation workers during the colonial period. (c) Explain why the Tamil-speakers of Sri Lanka do not behave as one single compact group.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: (a) Tamil-speakers are 18 per cent and are divided into two sub-groups. (b) Indian Tamils. (c) One sub-group consists of natives of the country, concentrated in the north and east, while the other descends from forefathers who came from India as plantation workers during the colonial period, so they have different origins and locations.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.stem:
The minority French-speaking community in Belgium was relatively rich and powerful. This was resented by the Dutch-speaking community, who got the benefit of economic development and education much later. This resentment led to tensions between the Dutch-speaking and French-speaking communities during the 1950s and 1960s. The tension between the two communities was more acute in Brussels, because there the Dutch speakers were a minority. If the Dutch community took advantage of its numeric majority and forced its will on the French and German-speaking populations, the conflict would be pushed further.

(a) Which community in Belgium was relatively rich and powerful, and which community resented it? (b) During which period did the tensions between the two communities appear? (c) Explain why a political settlement in which one community simply forces its will on the others is dangerous for Belgium.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: (a) The French-speaking minority was relatively rich and powerful, and the Dutch-speaking community resented it. (b) During the 1950s and 1960s. (c) The Dutch community's numeric majority could be used to force its will on the French and German speakers, which would push the conflict among the communities further.
